author: magrane
body: The Nature paper says "Protein sequences were obtained from the UniProt Reference Proteomes resource, which selects one canonical protein sequence per protein coding gene in each genome". But I checked with our developer who produces these sets and he said that the 2 TrEMBL entries you mentioned have not been canonical since at least 2020 and probably not since the beginning. There's a file of additional sequences which they are part of but they're not in the file of canonical sequences.

author: magrane
body: A0A2R8Y5L6 is part of the human reference proteome but not part of the '1 entry per gene' proteome. There are 2 versions of the proteome produced. One version contains a representative entry for each protein-coding gene. The other version contains the representative entries plus additional isoforms so there may be multiple records from the same gene. There's some more information about this at https://www.uniprot.org/help/human_proteome.

author: ValWood
body:
It seems confusing to have non-functional fragments  part of any reference proteome.
Or to have Trembl entries as part of  the human reference proteome. These 2, A0A2R8Y5L6 and A0A0D9SG24 (and I saw others) aren't associated with proteins with HGNC names, so it is difficult for users to understand what they are, why they are there (or to attempt to remove redundancy).

It's also difficult to get a handle on the Unknownome when these non functional fragments persist.

author: magrane
body: Hi Val, The human reference proteome contains many TrEMBL entries. The full proteome is at https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb?query=proteome:UP000005640 and you can see that there are 20,402 Swiss-Prot entries plus 62,983 TrEMBL entries. This is because many users want a proteome with all splice variants, not just a single representative entry for each gene. I'll check with the developers responsible for generating the proteome about the inclusion of the fragment entries and get back to you later about that.

author: magrane
body: Hi Val, to answer your question about fragments in the human proteome, the UniProt human reference proteome includes Swiss-Prot records plus all TrEMBL records imported from Ensembl including fragments as these represent additional isoforms.

This is the one linked from the "Gene count" section. There is some information about how this is produced at https://www.uniprot.org/help/gene_centric_isoform_mapping.
